maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext:
By leave of the house-and I think the house generally would agree that leave, in a case such as this, should be granted-I wish to mention the presence in the gallery of the Prime Minister of Japan, Hon. Nobusuke Kishi and, with him, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Hon. Aiichiro Fujiyama.
This is the first occasion on which this house has been visited by a prime minister of Japan. Our country has had long relations with our nearest neighbour to the west. Seventy years ago the first consular post by Japan was established in Canada, and Canada, on her part, established in Japan one of Canada's first diplomatic missions. On behalf of all hon. members in all parts of the house I wish to express a hearty welcome to these two distinguished visitors, coupled with the hope that their stay with us will be as productive as it has already been enjoyable to us.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition and of myself I should like to associate ourselves with the words the Prime Minister has just uttered, words of welcome to the Prime Minister of Japan, the foreign minister and the members of their party. It is quite true, as the Prime Minister said, that this is the first occasion on which a Prime Minister of Japan has visited our House of Commons. In that respect, at least, we are ahead of Japan, because I think I am right in saying that two Canadian prime ministers have had the honour of visiting Japan besides one who hopes, one day, to be prime minister.
Our lines of development, interest and contact have, in this country, because of our history, been in the past primarily across the Atlantic ocean to Europe. But in recent years we have learned, and we are still learning, that we are also a Pacific nation; and in the development of our Pacific contacts I am sure nothing has given greater pleasure to Canadians than the growth of close and friendly relations between Canada and that other great Pacific power, Japan. We have now
reached the point where our interests, economic and otherwise, are most important to each other and we all, I am sure, want to keep it that way.
Therefore it gives me very great pleasure indeed to associate our party with the words of welcome to our visitors which the Prime Minister has addressed to them both on their own behalf and on behalf of the great country they represent.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF JAPAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the C.C.F. party I wish to welcome our two distinguished visitors, Hon. Nobusuke Kishi, Prime Minister of Japan, and Hon. Aiichiro Fujiyama, the Minister of Foreign Affairs. We are pleased with the friendly relations that exist between Canada and Japan. We are hopeful that in the future trade between our two great countries will continue to develop. We realize that it is in the economic sphere that friendly, peaceful relationships can best flourish. We are pleased to see trade between Canada and Japan growing and indicating great promise for the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-32, to authorize provisional payments for the 1959-60 crop year in respect of unthreshed grain in the prairie provinces.
He said: In speaking to the resolution I set forth the harvesting position in the west. As nearly as can be ascertained there are about 100 million bushels of unthreshed grain in the three prairie provinces and in areas in British Columbia which fall within the designated area.
It is in connection with this 100 million bushels that the government has brought forward this bill. While the extent of the problem has decreased in the past two and one half months, many individual producers

face great difficulties because they have not been able to complete their harvesting. The bill is directed primarily to producers in this position.
This legislation is essentially of a short term nature. In very simple terms, it proposes that producers with unthreshed grain from the 1959 crop will be able to apply for limited provisional payments pending the completion of harvesting. These funds will be available to producers through their local elevator agents between the date on which the legislation is proclaimed and May 1 next. It is hoped that the provisional payments taken by producers will be fully repaid out of one half of the proceeds of their deliveries during the balance of the crop year.
The legislation before the house contains most of the provisions of the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act with which members of the house are familiar. These provisions are necessary to provide: (a) the necessary funds; (b) procedures whereby producers may secure provisional payments; (c) the basis upon which provisional payments will be authorized; and (d) the procedures relating to repayment of the provisional payments.
Basically, the formula under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act has been preserved. The amount of a provisional payment will be calculated on the basis of one half of the unthreshed grain multiplied by 50 cents per bushel in the case of wheat, 20 cents per bushel for oats and 35 cents per bushel for barley; provided that the one half of the unthreshed grain does not exceed the quantity which will be deliverable under a general quota of 6 bushels per specified acre less a deduction for prior deliveries. Up to this point the formula generally follows the pattern of the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act with which producers and elevator agents are familiar.
In the case of the present legislation, however, another factor will enter into the determining of a provisional payment. The quantity of threshed grain which the applying producer has in store on his farm will also be deducted. The reason for this deduction is that a producer can secure an advance payment on threshed grain under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act, and advances on threshed grain should be exclusively under that act. The producer will therefore be applying for an advance solely on that quantity of unthreshed grain which falls within the limitations which I have described.
The repayment provisions are similar to those under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act, with one exception. Under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act deliveries under the unit or initial quota are exempt from the repayment provisions of 79951-0-12
Advance Payments to Grain Producers the act. This legislation is being enacted at the half-way point of the crop year and, in order to facilitate the discharge of the producer's obligation promptly, one half the proceeds of all deliveries subsequent to the date of the producer's application for a provisional payment will be applied on repayment. I should add that at the present time, all delivery points are now off the unit quota and in most instances the unit quota has already been delivered even in those districts where there is considerable unthreshed grain still in the fields.
I can summarize the operation of the formula very briefly:
1.	If one half of a producer's unthreshed grain is less than the quantity which he would deliver on a 6-bushel general quota, then his maximum provisional payment is one half his unthreshed grain multiplied by 50 cents, 35 cents and 20 cents per bushel respectively for wheat, barley and oats, less the deductions to which I have referred.
2.	If one half his unthreshed grain is more than he can deliver under a 6-bushel general quota, then the maximum of his provisional payment is the quantity of grain he can deliver under a 6-bushel general quota multiplied by 50 cents, 35 cents and 20 cents per bushel respectively for wheat, barley and oats, less the deductions to which I have referred.
3.	The maximum provisional payment on unthreshed grain is $1,500.
I would like to say a word about the maximum provisional payment of $1,500. The limit of $1,500 would be equal to 50 cents a bushel on the quantity of wheat a producer could deliver under a 6-bushel general quota from a specified acreage of 500 acres. In 1958-59 the wheat board issued 227,000 permits. Of these permits 188,000 or 81 per cent showed a specified acreage of 500 acres or less. I believe these observations place the maximum limits under this legislation in proper perspective.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I wonder if the minister will allow me to interrupt him. I have been waiting for the house to settle down and give its attention to this debate. It seems to be noisier than usual. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The main safeguard in the case of cash advances under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act, and in the case of provisional payments under the present bill, is the endorsement on a producer's permit book when a cash advance or a provisional payment is made to him. Once an endorsement is on the permit book all elevator
170	HOUSE OF
Advance Payments to Grain Producers agents are required to deduct one half the proceeds of deliveries of wheat, oats or barley delivered under the permit book for remittance to the wheat board in repayment of the cash advance and/or the provisional payment. From experience we know that this type of security is effective, and is respected by producers who take cash advances. Over and beyond this there is an undertaking on the part of producers under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act and in the present bill that they will deliver grain in sufficient quantity to repay cash advances or provisional payments as delivery quotas are made available to them.
When this bill has been enacted a producer with threshed grain will, as in the past, be eligible to apply for a cash advance up to a maximum of $3,000 under the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act; a producer with unharvested grain will be eligible to obtain a provisional payment up to a maximum of $1,500 under the proposed legislation; and a producer with both threshed and unthreshed grain may use both statutes subject to a maximum of $1,500 for unthreshed grain and up to an over-all maximum of $3,000.
The government has introduced the present bill at this time with confidence that its prompt enactment by parliament will be welcomed by many farmers and their families in western Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preceding this bill was under discussion on January 19, several speakers from this side of the house including myself indicated that it was their intention to support this bill. As the minister said, in essence it simply provides the same form of cash payments under the machinery of the wheat board and its agents with respect to unthreshed grain in western Canada that is provided with respect to threshed grain under the provisions of the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act.
As such it obviously is not a form of agricultural assistance that it is likely could be utilized by other producers in other parts of the country, because the grain that is subject to the advance payments under this bill is grain as defined by the Canadian Wheat Board Act and the area where the benefits will apply is, of course, the geographical section as described in the wheat board act.
This legislation appears to be reasonable, because the producers of grain, as defined by the Canadian Wheat Board Act, are in a different category with respect to payments from other agricultural producers in the country, particularly with respect to two


features relating to their activities and production. In the first place they are under compulsion to deliver their produce, namely the three grains named in the wheat board act and in this bill, to the government agency, the Canadian wheat board. In addition, as all hon. members realize, those particular products do not benefit from any form of price support.
Therefore, while there was some discussion on Tuesday last about the desirability of at all times, when presenting legislation, ensuring that it will have national effect and benefit, perhaps in connection with this legislation that is not as appropriate as some might have thought. No one would have any quarrel with national application as a basic principle, but this particular bill deals with produce that is under compulsory marketing in accordance with a government statute, and it deals only with the western grain producers who are subject to that act with respect to three grains.
Now, we are dealing with this legislation on an emergency basis, having interrupted in the early stages of this new session other business that normally is proceeded with in the first ten days of the session. As was indicated the other day, we over here are well aware that this is just one of several forms of assistance that it is felt will meet the deplorable situation that we are all aware has been existing in western Canada by reason of the early snows that made it impossible to harvest the western grain crops and other crops in a normal fashion.
I was disappointed to hear from the minister in introducing this bill at this stage no reference to the discussion we had the other day which I thought was reasonable, to the effect that we have agreed to give emergency attention to this bill and another bill that will follow when this debate concludes. We indicated that from the press we had learned that there are other forms of proposed government assistance, of which we officially know nothing although we have been in session now for a week. Since the aid contemplated in this bill and in the second bill which will follow this one is not likely to involve the taxpayers of this country in any expenditure of great consequence, though there is the likelihood that the other form of aid in co-operation with the provinces, about which we can get information only in the newspapers, will be something of substance, we reiterate that we think it is, as I said the other day, a contempt of parliament to by-pass us in this way so that in some leisurely fashion, at a time that suits the

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
government, they can bring on discussion on the other important matter in the form of an estimate.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that under this kind of procedure we are surely being asked simply to shadow-box with reality. 1 think it is obvious that while we are supporting this legislation we have every reason to be indignant. We are indignant, it is so clear that the government and the Prime Minister particularly, who has had so much to say in the past about parliamentary rights, are making a cat's paw of this parliament in connection with this agricultural relief program for western Canada in this emergency.
There is as I say, Mr. Speaker, no quarrel with the content of the bill which, in its provisions and in the contemplated machinery for making the advance payments, so closely parallels legislation with which most of us now are so familiar and which has been working very satisfactorily indeed. I do want to say that the advance payments legislation is operating very satisfactorily. I would in no way quarrel with the experience we have had with it for a couple of years. I can well understand that members of the government are pleased to take credit for that legislation and for such merit as it has.
However, I do want to point out to the house, and particularly to the agricultural constituencies in western Canada, that we learned on Tuesday just what it actually means in expense to the crown. I think in each of the three years we have had this form of advance payments in operation the actual cost to the federal government, to the taxpayers, has been only about $450,000 annually.
On the other hand, while it was rather disparaged, the legislation of the previous government with respect to the assumption of storage costs for grain in excess of 178 million bushels a year is, as experience shows, worth somewhere between $35 million and $40 million each year to western grain producers.
I will have further comments to make in connection with the individual sections of the bill, Mr. Speaker. Again I was disappointed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who avoided something that I think was legitimate questioning on our part when I referred to a desire to obtain in the house some detail as to the extent to which it had been found possible to assist in this emergency in another way. The Prime Minister, when he talked to the press about introducing this particular bill, also indicated a possibility that money would be put into circulation at a more rapid pace by speeding up the payment provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

I say that when this house is considering the plight of the western grain producers, and we are asked to pass this bill, we are entitled to find out whether it is adequate assistance. We cannot find out whether it is adequate and whether it is meeting the need unless this house is taken into the confidence of the government and we receive information to which we are properly entitled with respect to payments under P.F.A.A. and with respect to the payments that are proposed to be made through the instrumentality of the provinces on a 50-50 cost sharing basis relative to relief payments.
In addition to that I think the Prime Minister, when he issued the press release, also made reference to the assistance that will be given also through the instrumentality of the provinces with respect to the movement of fodder because of the need that arises by reason of the early and heavy snows in western Canada. I asked the Minister of Agriculture on Tuesday-he is not with us today-for information as to what relief is already in motion. He displayed a considerable lack of knowledge of that very important aspect, and I then suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that since he came from Manitoba perhaps he could comment at least on some press reports I spoke of indicating nothing was being paid out yet in Manitoba, the western province that I know best.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation introduces some very logical amendments to the cash advance statute now in effect, and makes it possible for the Canadian wheat board to provide advances, with the permit books as security, to farmers who have grain under the snow. This legislation is possible because over the years western producers have had the foresight to market their grain through a public marketing board, and the machinery that is available under the Canadian Wheat Board Act lends itself very readily to such legislation as is before us today.
In discussing this legislation I think we should keep in mind the amount of money that is likely to be involved as far as the individual farmer is concerned, and what the total outlay is likely to be. As the minister has said, the individual maximum is $1,500, and in the context of an advance on a 6-bushel quota the fact, as the minister pointed out, that this will make it possible for 80 per cent of the farmers to receive the maximum amount as far as their acreage is concerned means that it is probably a reasonable ceiling.
But having said that may I say that I think this demonstrates very vividly the economic position in which western farmers
172	HOUSE OF
Advance Payments to Grain Producers find themselves. Just imagine any urban group suffering a loss of income and coming to the federal parliament to ask for legislation which would provide them with an emergency gross income of only $1,500. The fact is that our western farmers will have a maximum of $1,500 out of which to pay all their living expenses and carry on their farming operations until next April or May. We know that with the gross national product going up the average income earner expects to get something like $4,000 a year, and that without many expenses attached to earning such income. Yet the people who are in the business of producing grain and who have a heavy investment in land and machinery are so destitute that they are pleased when the government introduces legislation to provide them with the opportunity of getting even a small sum of money as an advance.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Even on the relief scheme Premier Roblin says it will only pay the taxes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
This is really just a relief
measure for an industry that is in financial jeopardy and has looked to the government for some assistance. The Prime Minister talked of a great vision, of a new Canada in which all industries and all groups would receive equitable treatment and a fair share of the national income. I do not think there is any part of Canada where the vision has disappeared so rapidly as it has in the prairie provinces where the people live who are affected by such legislation as this.
I asked previously that the government, together with this type of measure, provide deficiency payments on western grain, and immediately there was objection from the government side of the house. It was said, what if a man did not produce any grain? I would imagine that if deficiency payments were made they would put cash into the hands of about 99 per cent of the farmers now involved, and without forcing them to repay. They would have it as of right without having to repay. In my opinion the government has betrayed western agriculture by failing to act in this regard.
In my view the legislation now before us is not likely to be used by the majority of the farmers who could qualify for payments. I say that because of the history of the cash advance legislation itself. I am all in favour of the legislation because undoubtedly some farmers will use it, but I contend that the majority of farmers are not likely to make very much use of it.
The minister pointed out in the house, as recorded on page 119 of Hansard, the very limited use that had been made of the cash advance legislation, and I use the word "limited" in relation to the proportion of


farmers who were entitled to such cash advances. Some 45,000 to 50,000 farmers have obtained advances in each year of the three year period, and total advances amount to something like $35 million. This means that about 20 per cent of the farmers who are permit book holders are taking advantage of the legislation. It seems a very good business proposition that a farmer should have the opportunity to get an interest-free cash advance in the fall against grain to be delivered some months later, usually almost a year later. It would look like very good business on their part, and I think those people who are active in the financial field would advise every farmer to rush in and get a cash advance and save the interest.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I think either the hon. member is under a misapprehension or we are. Is he suggesting that all these people in the northern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan who feed grains rather than sell them are necessarily in need of cash advances, and that they will take advantage of the legislation? Does he say that 100 per cent of the farmers must necessarily qualify?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
One hundred per cent of the farmers who have permit books qualify. There are farmers in the prairies who do not have permit books because they feed all their grain. Therefore they do not qualify and would not ask for such advances. But if a farmer is delivering as little as 100 bushels of wheat a year he must have a permit book, and if he has a permit book he is entitled under the regulations to ask for a cash advance after taking into account the unit quota. You have to have a permit book to come under this legislation, and one would think that farmers generally who have permit books would rush to the elevators to get this interest-free money -especially farmers in Alberta, I would think, because interest-free money has been such a popular thing there for so long in the minds of many people.
But 80 per cent of the farmers did not take advantage of the interest-free money. Why? That is an interesting question. I have been asking farmers why, and this is the answer I get. They say that they are short of money and would like a cash advance, but if they take a cash advance then next spring when they deliver their grain, at a time when they have a great many expenses in seeding their crops, they can only get approximately half the proceeds and are placed in an impossible financial position. From a business standpoint the farmer is actually sacrificing the amount of interest-free money that is involved in such advances because he does not want to put himself in the position of being able to get only one half the value of his grain in cash when he makes delivery in the spring.

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
The result is that under the present government the financial position of the prairie grain farmers has not improved but has in fact worsened with the steady increase in the farmers' costs of production. Cash advance legislation, in my opinion, is good legislation. As I have said, it has only been used to the extent of 20 per cent or 25 per cent of those eligible, but that still brings a good deal of benefit to a great many producers.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) made the statement that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Conservative government could take credit for the cash advance legislation. Well, certainly the Liberal party could not take any credit for it, because they sat over there with their arms folded for about 20 years when this was a very important problem. They said, "You cannot do it; it will not work". The former minister of trade and commerce said the wheat board would resign, so everybody thought that would be a great calamity to see the wheat board resign. Then we asked for the correspondence. We asked for the exact statements of the wheat board, and we found that the statements, in the main, were in the mind of the minister. The wheat board did not resign. Under this administration they are still very much the same efficient people who were operating it under the former administration, and the legislation has worked out.
I should like to know from the minister the amount of absolute loss entailed in cash advances under this legislation, and the percentage of advances that have not been recovered, that are in arrears, and that it is expected will be written off. I would think it would be a very insignificant percentage, because the risk involved is very slight indeed.
Sometimes government members get rather impatient with the members who sit over here when they take part in extended debates. Members who are in this parliament for the first time really have not seen an opposition that is operating as an opposition. They should have sat in the gallery a few years ago when we had the bank loans legislation before us, and they would have seen an opposition that fought that legislation for three weeks. Government members of the day were very impatient with us. The names they called us; the terrible things they said to us in the elevators as we went up to our offices after the debates were over. There is some of that impatience now, though this impatience does not take so long to come to the fore.
When the bank loans legislation was first introduced, members of the C.C.F. group in the house fought it. We fought it for many
days. At first the Conservatives said they were going to support it; then they switched, because they found that supporting the bank loan legislation was not too popular. We attempted to get the government to introduce cash advances, but they refused and the electorate took steps to see that this condition was changed.
We have, therefore, made some progress in this regard, and we in this group believe it was, partly at any rate, because of the very active part we took in the debate some years ago. If the Liberal party was wiped out on the prairies because it failed to listen to the producers, I think this government could lose a tremendous amount of support in the prairies. I do not believe they will be wiped out, mind you; there will be a few survivors, but I think they could lose many seats, particularly in the rural constituencies of the three prairie provinces, if they fail to heed the united voice of the prairies requesting financial assistance that is not repayable but that takes into account the tremendous increase in the cost of production without any compensation by way of increase in the prices for their products during the past 15 years.
I wish the government had introduced the third piece of legislation, the third measure that must be undertaken in order to round out the program of assistance to western Canada. As has already been announced, this government along with the provincial governments will bear the cost of making these payments. I feel that in a national emergency, as I think this is, it is the national government that should act. I believe this government is too much inclined to ask for cost-sharing arrangements with the provincial governments. There is no cost-sharing arrangement with the provincial governments under prairie farm assistance. We feel that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act could have been used to a much greater extent. First of all, it could have been considered a crop failure where all the grain is under the snow. I do not believe I would want to go that far, because if the farmers are fortunate enough to get out their grain next spring I do not see why they should have that kind of consideration; that would be a little too much.
However, I do feel that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should have been made to apply next spring on an individual basis to those farmers who have lost their crops. The farmer cannot pull a tarpaulin over his crop to hide it; he cannot go out during the night and carry it away to show that he did not have a crop when, in fact, he did. It would be a very simple thing for inspectors to go out through western Canada about next May or

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (for ihe Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR SHORT TERM LOANS TO GRAIN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made before the 1st day of June, 1960, for short term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to thresh their grain; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the Act shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: PROVISION FOR SHORT TERM LOANS TO GRAIN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
This resolution forecasts a bill which will supplement the Prairie Grain Provisional Payments Act, just passed. Its purpose is to assist prairie grain producers who are in financial difficulties because of the abnormal harvest conditions during the current crop year. The bill to be founded on the resolution will make provision for government guaranteed bank loans on the security of both threshed and unthreshed grain. The loan measure, together with the bill just passed, is further evidence, if I may say so, of the government's determination to help prairie farmers who have been able to deliver little or no grain in this crop year.
Turning to the main features of the proposed legislation, it may suffice at this stage to indicate that all producers will be able to obtain a short term bank loan in respect of a wide range of grain crops, wheat, oats, barley, rye, flaxseed and rapeseed. Repayment will be made out of deliveries and the producers will be required to assign to the bank one half of the proceeds from the sale of their grain. Loans may be obtained at any
182	HOUSE OF
Short Term Loans to Grain Producers time up to June 1, 1960. A maximum limit of $1,500 will be placed upon loans to any one farmer. The banks will calculate individual loan entitlement on the basis of one half of the estimated value of the grain which the producer expects to deliver in the course of the crop year.
In order to encourage bank lending under this program, each bank will be guaranteed against loss up to 25 per cent of the aggregate loans made where this does not exceed $150,000. A guarantee of 20 per cent will be applicable to the total loans made by each bank in excess of $150,000. There will, of course, be a maximum limit on the aggregate guaranteed loans to all banks, and this will amount to $50 million.
I might just repeat in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that this bill supplements the legislation just passed authorizing provisional payment by the Canadian wheat board in respect of unthreshed grain. As explained, loans may be made on rapeseed in addition to those grains which are marketed through the Canadian wheat board. This will provide a means and opportunity, on a comprehensive basis, whereby the producer can improve his cash position. As a result, the government's proposal should prove to be of material assistance in alleviating the temporary financial difficulties due to the interruption of the harvesting operation in western Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR SHORT TERM LOANS TO GRAIN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I first take this opportunity to extend my personal congratulations, and those of the members in this party, to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, who has just stood up before us this session for the first time since his official appointment. We recall how competently he fulfilled the duties of that position in the 1957 session. Some of us were very disappointed indeed that it was not seen fit to restore him to that position in 1958, but better late than never. We know that he will fulfil his duties and assist the minister in a very worthy way.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I want to make some remarks on the resolution that is before us. I was disappointed that neither in the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the earlier debate nor in those of the parliamentary secretary now have we obtained what I feel is necessary and desirable recognition of our entitlement to some information about the balance of the program to assist the western farmer in the predicament in which he finds himself because of climatic conditions. I am exceedingly disappointed in this. I do not know when we have been more badly treated in this manner. There seems to me to have been a quite unnecessary amount of legerdemain in treating


parliament in this hanky-panky fashion. Surely it is important to provide us with some information about the cost-sharing plan with the provinces as a basis for properly appreciating the adequacy and justification of this measure. I regard the other as the more important form of assistance to western agriculture under present conditions. We are not getting any information about it.
I feel that this is certainly not something one would have expected from a party that had so much to say recently about parliamentary rights. Not very long ago I was talking to one of the candidates of the Conservative party who was not successful but who, however, has been observing the government from outside the house. I can assure the government this particular candidate was looking rather sadly upon actions of the government such as the by-passing of parliament we are experiencing in connection with this western farm legislation. The only comment that this unsuccessful candidate had to make about the government and the Progressive Conservative party and the change in attitude that seemed to be displayed in matters like this was, "Well, unfortunately power seems to corrupt."
Mr. Chairman, we are told nothing about the base of assistance being provided in another measure in western Canada. We are told now about one of the measures-one of four, only two of which are presented to us-which deals with bank guaranteed loans. This is rather interesting because we had a similar, if not identical situation in 1951. I think the hon. member for Wetaskiwin said the situation today was quite different from previous seasons when there were also misfortunes in the west because of early onslaught of snow. But in any event, 1951 presented a serious problem similar to that we are discussing today.
The minister of trade and commerce at that time, Mr. Howe, introduced what was called the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act, 1951. Not only has this government changed its attitude with respect to the rights of parliament and particularly the rights of opposition members, but it seems, in recommending this legislation to us at this time, to have changed very radically its position with respect to the merits of guaranteed bank loans to western farmers. Indeed, it seems to have radically changed its views as to the commercial merit of making loans with respect to grain that is either still standing or under snow during winter.
This afternoon the hon. member for As-siniboia was endeavouring to present to some of the new members of the house a comparison of the attitude of the present members

on the government side when they were sitting in opposition with the attitude that they, and particularly the new members, are adopting when there seems to be any desire to have even a minimum of discussion about some of these matters. They are impatient when we say we are exceedingly annoyed when we are by-passed with respect to a proposition as important as that offered to the western provinces in connection with relief to western farmers.
In 1951, when we had a proposition from Mr. Howe along these lines, I would like to give the new hon. members of the house an idea of the kind of obstruction and opposition presented at that time. Everything was wrong with the legislation. We have not taken that attitude this afternoon at all. We have said that we are supporting this legislation. We have said we also accept the legislation preceding this. We have indicated we are prepared to accept this legislation for what it is worth.
By the way, may I say the legislation in 1951 due to a fall weather emergency was introduced, much earlier than has been made possible this time. The bank loans legislation then was introduced to the house on December 14. Again in 1956 when certain relief was necessary, parliament even made the guarantee retroactive from January back to loans which were encouraged from the middle of November, 1955 when the need was urgent.
I want to present the view of the present Prime Minister with respect to the value to western Canada of bank guaranteed loans to farmers, particularly with respect to wheat lying on the ground under snow. This is what he said, as reported on page 1970 of Hansard of December 14, 1951:
I am sure the banks will make no advances against wheat laying on the ground, having regard to the probable toughness of that wheat next spring. I think in a case such as that there should be some provision whereby payments similar in nature to those under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would be made available to farmers.
A few minutes before that as reported on page 1969 of Hansard, this was the Prime Minister's view as to the merit of guaranteed bank loans with respect to grain under snow:
I now come to the third matter, and that is in connection with the farmer who has not been able to thresh his crop, whose crop today is either standing in the fields or lying on the ground in swaths. I am not suggesting and I have not at any time suggested that there should be loans made on crops under those conditions, for there would be a considerable risk.
The amused comment of Mr. Howe immediately following that remark of the present Prime Minister was this:
Yet we are doing it.
Short Term Loans to Grain Producers
That was the kind of scoffing and opposition we got with respect to legislation of this kind.
Then again in 1956, with respect to the amount of advances that might be made under a guaranteed bank loan, the present Minister of Agriculture had a great deal of sneering to do. As indicated on page 627 of Hansard for January 27, 1956, he complained that the interest rate-which, by the way, was 5 per cent-was not justified; he said it should not be more than 3 per cent. He said:
The next point is that the maximum amount of $1,500 by way of a loan is too small. It is not sufficient to meet the farmer's harvesting expenses and carry him through the winter
That was the kind of quibbling opposition we got in those days with respect to any proposition to aid western farmers with guaranted bank loans.
I say, look at the contrast now. We are giving the government co-operation in a desire that any aid that is possible at this late date after the emergency has arisen will be dealt with by this parliament. But it does not reduce in any way our expectation of, and entitlement to information with respect to all other methods of relief to deal with the same emergency and the same conditions, and we reiterate that in this respect we are being by-passed.
I now want to indicate to all hon. members that, contrary to the view held by the present Prime Minister in 1951 that the risk would be considerable and that there was a very dubious value in making an advance to western farmers for grain under snow, I think the record shows that assistance of value was given, and that the loss to the taxpayers was relatively small indeed. I think the words of Mr. Howe at that time were borne out; I share the view he expressed then, now. At page 1968 of Hansard of December 14, 1951, when that legislation which the present Prime Minister scoffed at was being introduced, Mr. Howe said:
-these loans are not in any sense to be regarded as a form of relief. They are interim advances made available at commercial rates of interest to producers who have grain on their farms or who have crops which they have every reason to believe will be harvested in due course.
In connection with loans of this kind, the Minister of Agriculture in 1956 sneered at anything in the nature of a rate of interest at commercial rates. He indicated that the farmer was being abused if he paid even 5 per cent in connection with a government guaranteed bank loan.
In addition to that, I would like to know from the parliamentary secretary-perhaps we will have to wait for the bill-what the
184	HOUSE OF
Short Term Loans to Grain Producers proposal is with respect to interest under this legislation. Certainly one of the features that in the past has always excited hon. members who now sit on the government side was any suggestion that the rate of interest would be not disclosed to parliament, and that it might be left to the discretion and judgement of the cabinet. Having in mind their strong views of the past in this respect, I hope that we will not find that they are in any way departing from the old stand they used to take in this as they have departed in some of these other matters.
I do feel that at this stage it is also proper to ask the parliamentary secretary for information as to the experience of the last measure which provided guaranteed bank loans to western farmers. I refer to the legislation entitled the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act of 1956. When the cash advances were provided in 1957, Mr. Gardiner, the former minister of agriculture, was then in the house, in opposition and in supporting the cash advance legislation he indicated to the new government that, in his opinion, there was considerable value in maintaining alongside the new legislation the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act. Indeed, the former government, in the spring of 1957, took steps to make sure that that legislation would not lapse.
The parliamentary secretary has indicated that, unlike the bill we passed a short time ago, the type of grain eligible for some financial assistance under this bill is considerably wider. The other bill restricted advances to crops under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board, but here, as the parliamentary secretary pointed out, in addition to grain such as wheat, oats and barley it will be possible for banks to make loans and have them guaranteed by the federal government on flaxseed, rapeseed and rye. Rye was covered by the legislation of 1956, and I wonder if a spokesman for the government would indicate why this legislation of
1956,	extended in 1957 by the former government, was allowed to lapse, because there was in the provisions of that bill an opportunity for bank guaranteed loans in respect of grains which have no eligibility for cash advances under the advance payment act of
1957.	Perhaps, also, the parliamentary secretary would give us any information he has on crown losses with respect to the 1951 and 1956 bank guaranteed loans legislation.
Here we have before us legislation in connection with farm credit. I think there are a great many farmers who are re-reading somewhat ruefully some of the advertisements
[Mr. Benidlckson.l

about credit which were made by the Conservative party in the recent election campaign. I have in my hands an advertisement from the Family Herald, dated March 27, 1958 and I quote:
As promised, the government is now moving to ease farm credit as such. The general easing of the credit situation has already benefited the farm economy.
We know that the discount rate at the central bank then was about 2.52 per cent and at that time, as on so many other occasions, the government took credit for the lowering of that rate. They said they had created a general easing of the credit situation which had benefited the farmers. But today they run away and say the commercial banks or the central bank or someone else must bear the responsibility for the fact that the discount rate is practically double what it was at the time they were making those boasts and taking credit for a reduction in the rate. It is hoped that in the stringent money market of the moment experienced by farmers, along with all others in other segments of the economy, this legislation will be of some value to those it is intended to benefit.
We will have questions to ask about the rate of interest and certain other provisions when we see the bill, but unlike the type of opposition shown in respect to these matters in the past by those who are now sitting on the treasury benches we are prepared to support something that is going to give some aid to the western farmer in present conditions. We will not put up a lot of petty objections to every single feature in connection with the bill as the Prime Minister and some of his friends did in days gone by, indicating that they were not satisfied with the interest rate, the amount of the loan, or anything else and suggesting that there was not a tittle of value in anything which was done by the government through the banks to aid western farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR SHORT TERM LOANS TO GRAIN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
In listening to the parliamentary secretary one would have thought that very large sums of money-exceedingly large sums-would likely be made available under this legislation. However, as I see it this is merely a companion measure to the one already passed. I regard it as a minor measure compared with that other bill, and consider that only a small minority of farmers are likely to be in a position to borrow money under its terms. I should like to know from the parliamentary secretary or from the Minister of Finance whether or not a farmer who has obtained a cash advance under the bill just passed is entitled to a guaranteed bank loan, because if farmers who have obtained cash advances for grain under the

Short Term Loans to Grain Producers
snow are excluded from this legislation then, of course, this measure will apply only to a very small proportion of the farmers.
The Minister of Finance is in the house. He has been very vocal in the past. He has been a valiant scrapper for the rights of parliament. He, and the Prime Minister, when they were in opposition, spent a large part of their time on this theme. They complained about everything which in their opinion interfered with or by-passed parliamentary control. I think we have a justifiable reason for complaining to the government today about the gratuitous insult to parliament and the insult to the prairie producers which is constituted by the failure to come forward with an estimate or legislation which would provide the acreage payments for grain under the snow.
Parliament is in session. The government should take parliament into its confidence. We have a right to know from the government and from the Minister of Finance the exact extent to which the government is committed to payments for grain under the snow by way of cash assistance. The rights of parliament, so dear to the government in the past, have become a plaything today. Parliament is a plaything. The consideration of the address in reply to the speech from the throne was interrupted at the convenience of the government and resumed again at the government's convenience, which shows just how co-operative the opposition is in this regard. But the government is in contempt of parliament because it will not divulge the commitments which it has already made to the provinces, the amount of those commitments and the type of legislation it intends to introduce.
I wonder why the Minister of Finance is not recommending that this legislation should be introduced at the present time. I think a good case could have been made in late October, November or early December for calling parliament into session in order to deal with this emergency; to pass the legislation which we are now considering and introduce legislation to provide for payments direct to the producers in respect of grain under the snow. That was not done. Instead, the government has waited until well into the new year before calling parliament into session. But with parliament in session the government persists in insulting parliament, in by-passing the house and forgetting all the speeches which were made in the past about the rights of hon. members.
There is only one conclusion at which one can arrive, that the government now has no consideration for the rights of parliament, that all those speeches in the past were phony speeches, fabricated for the day, or
put forward merely to attempt to persuade the public that members of the Conservative party really believed in the rights of parliament, because now they are in a position to defend parliament and to show that they meant what they said a few years ago.

But what else did our government do? At the first possible moment after the session started-incidentally, the matter was mentioned in the speech from the throne-the legislation was brought before parliament and parliament was given a chance to consider it. Now, that is what we are objecting to. We are not objecting, and no one here has objected, to the undertaking given by the Prime Minister. Perhaps in form it might have been a little more scrupulously given; perhaps the Prime Minister in giving it might have shown a little more consideration for the paramount position of parliament, but I am not making much of that. But what I am making something of, and what I think everybody in the opposition is making something of and what everybody now occupying the treasury benches, and no one more than the Minister of Finance, should be making something of is the fact that at any rate one of the western provinces is paying out money, half of which the Prime Minister of this country has said will be repaid out of the treasury of Canada. parliamentary secretary to hedge. There would be no reason for the Minister of Finance to remain silent. There would be no reason for the bill not to have a clause saying that the interest rate will be 5 per cent.
In other words, the banks have vetoed any legislation providing an interest rate of 5 per cent. Apparently the banks have said, "Nothing doing, we will have nothing to do any longer with legislation containing a fixed interest rate of 5 per cent." They have either said that or the government has not requested the banks to make money available at an interest rate of 5 per cent. If the banks today, on the basis of a guarantee of 25 per cent, will not make money available at an interest rate of 5 per cent we can only conclude that all our farm improvement legislation, fishermen's legislation and other legislation carrying with it a guarantee from the government and a fixed rate of 5 per cent is in fact in jeopardy.
When the members of the government were in the opposition they complained of the evils of a tight money policy and they were right. Everything they said at that time was correct and is just as correct today. The legislation now being introduced means a 20 per cent increase in interest rates over the guaranteed bank loan legislation of 1956. Instead of improvement, instead of a loosening, the money situation is getting tighter and interest rates are rising.
This legislation is a casualty of the policy of the government in fostering and promoting a high interest policy. Of course the Minister of Finance has been paying more than 6 per cent on some of his treasury bills so it is understandable that the banks should say no and veto the government's request if such a request was made. All I can do is protest as strongly as I can against the government's repudiation of everything its members said about tight money when they were in opposition. Now that they are following this very bad policy which they once condemned so loudly, the question arises whether or not this very definite indication in legislative form of higher interest rates is an indication of other acts of the government that may result in still higher interest rates.
To foist a 20 per cent increase in interest rates on agricultural producers is completely unjustified. The producers in my constituency grow flax to some extent but very little rapeseed is produced. I am wondering whether the members who represent constituencies in which rapeseed is an important crop will say anything about this retrograde and backward step, the increase in interest rates to farmers who will be forced to take
advantage of this legislation. I should like to hear from some of them whether or not they condone what amounts to a 20 per cent increase in interest rates within a period of four years.
We in this group will have something further to say on this matter when we are in committee on the bill and we shall put forward an amendment that we hope the house will approve asking that an interest rate of 5 per cent be fixed rather than the government pillorying the farmers by increasing interest rates by 20 per cent and making them less able to pay and victims of a vicious tight money policy. I see an ad hoc cabinet meeting going on over there. Three important cabinet ministers have their heads together. Two of them are prairie cabinet ministers and they might well have their heads together because this is an important question. I hope they will refer this matter to their colleagues in the cabinet and see that an amendment is introduced to get them off the hook because they are on the hook when they try to foist on the hard pressed people of their own provinces an increase in interest rates from 5 to 6 per cent. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is smiling. I do not think this is any smiling matter. He should look glum. He should look as glum as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who understands that this is a serious matter.

I have pointed out to the large number of members in the house who were not here either during the debate in 1956 or the debate in the spring of 1957 that we are shocked at the somersaulting that is being done with respect to so many of government policies. In 1956 the opposition of that day, the Conservative party, said it was unconscionable for farmers to pay an interest rate of 5 per cent. The present Minister of Agriculture went up and down this country saying that the interest rate should not be beyond 3 per cent. This was when an interest rate was in the bill but there were days of arguing.
The following year, there was an amendment which proposed to eliminate the fixed rate of interest in order that there might be what some hon. member referred to earlier as a commercial rate of interest which might be flexible. This was in the spring of 1957. What astonishes us is that the members of the government in power today seem to be prepared to abandon completely the things they held out to the people of this country as being important, almost sacred. I referred to and quoted part of the debate of 1956, but I might say there was a completely different situation in 1957. The other point is the aspect of not admitting in the bill what the rate is going to be. We know the maximum rate under the Bank Act is 6 per cent. If that is going to be paid, and there have been discussions with the banks, why does the government not have the courage to come and tell this House of Commons what the interest rate is likely to be? They said when they got into power they were going to do things differently, including stating in a bill of this kind what the rate of interest was going to be.
